summary: This document specifies conventions for using the Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA) in X.509 certificates and CRLs, including how keys and signatures are encoded. SLH-DSA is a post-quantum scheme standardized by NIST.

plainLanguage.summary: This tells certificates how to use a signature scheme built from hash functions, which is meant to withstand quantum computers.

questions: how are slh-dsa keys encoded in x509
what key usage bits does slh-dsa allow
subtitle: How to put hash-based, quantum-resistant SLH-DSA signatures and keys into X.509 certificates and CRLs.

tldr.problem: SLH-DSA is a quantum-resistant signature scheme standardized by NIST, but X.509 certificates and CRLs need agreed object identifiers and encodings before anyone can use it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns 24 algorithm identifiers (12 for Pure SLH-DSA, 12 for HashSLH-DSA), says the parameters field MUST be absent, and stores raw keys and signatures directly in BIT STRING and OCTET STRING fields.
tldr.outcome: Certificate authorities choose Pure or HashSLH-DSA up front, since a key tied to one kind of identifier cannot be used with the other.

today: RFC 9909 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2025, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It relies on RFC 9814 for the Pure SLH-DSA identifiers.

sections.title: What SLH-DSA Is and Why It Needs an RFC
sections.content:
The Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA) is a quantum-resistant signature scheme standardized in FIPS 205 by NIST's Post-Quantum Cryptography project. Before standardization it was known as SPHINCS+. The RFC states that SLH-DSA and SPHINCS+ are not compatible.

This document defines the ASN.1 object identifiers (OIDs) and the encoding conventions for SLH-DSA signatures, public keys and private keys in the X.509 Public Key Infrastructure. SLH-DSA offers three security levels, chosen to be at least as secure as a generic block cipher of 128, 192 or 256 bits. Each level comes in a small (s) and a fast (f) version, and can use either the SHA-2 family or SHAKE256 internally.

The fast versions are optimized for key generation and signing speed, but they are slower at verification than the small ones. The small versions are optimized for signature size.
sections.plainLanguage: SLH-DSA is a way to sign things using only scrambling functions. It comes in sizes and speeds, a bit like a choice between a small lock and a quick lock. This RFC says how certificates should label which one they use.

sections.title: Pure and Pre-Hash Modes
sections.content:
SLH-DSA has two signature modes. In pure mode, the whole content is signed directly. In pre-hash mode, a digest of the content is signed. The RFC calls these Pure SLH-DSA and HashSLH-DSA.

NIST has assigned separate identifiers for every combination of security level, fast versus small, SHA-2 versus SHAKE256, and pure versus pre-hash. SLH-DSA signing also takes an optional context string of at most 255 bytes. This document only specifies the empty context string, which is the default.

For HashSLH-DSA, the hash used for the pre-hash is named after the -with- part of the algorithm name. For example, id-hash-slh-dsa-sha2-128s-with-sha256 uses SHA-256. With SHAKE128 the pre-hash output is 256 bits, and with SHAKE256 it is 512 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: You can sign a whole letter, or you can sign a short summary of the letter. Both ways are allowed, but they use different labels so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
An AlgorithmIdentifier holds an object identifier in its algorithm field and an optional parameters field. The OIDs for SLH-DSA come from NIST's Computer Security Objects Register and sit under the sigAlgs arc. The same identifier names a public key, a private key and a signature.

The 12 Pure SLH-DSA identifiers are numbered 20 to 31 under sigAlgs (id-slh-dsa-sha2-128s is 20 and id-slh-dsa-shake-256f is 31). The 12 HashSLH-DSA identifiers are numbered 35 to 46 (id-hash-slh-dsa-sha2-128s-with-sha256 is 35 and id-hash-slh-dsa-shake-256f-with-shake256 is 46). The Pure OIDs are also defined in RFC 9814.

For every one of these algorithms, the parameters component MUST be absent.
sections.plainLanguage: Each flavor of SLH-DSA gets its own number, like a model number on a gadget. The label stands alone and needs no extra notes.

sections.title: Signatures, Public Keys and Private Keys
sections.content:
An SLH-DSA signature has three elements: R, SIG_FORS and SIG_HT. The raw signature is their concatenation, R || SIG_FORS || SIG_HT, and it goes straight into the signature BIT STRING with no extra ASN.1 wrapping. Signing and verifying use the algorithms from FIPS 205 (slh_sign and slh_verify for Pure, hash_slh_sign and hash_slh_verify for HashSLH-DSA).

A public key is two n-byte elements, PK.seed || PK.root, so it is 2*n bytes, where n is 16, 24 or 32 depending on the parameter set. In a SubjectPublicKeyInfo, the subjectPublicKey BIT STRING holds these raw bytes, and the algorithm identifier MUST be one of the id-slh-dsa-* or id-hash-slh-dsa-* OIDs with parameters absent.

A private key is four n-byte elements, SK.seed || SK.prf || PK.seed || PK.root, so it is 4*n bytes. It is carried in the privateKey OCTET STRING of a OneAsymmetricKey structure from RFC 5958. If the public key is included there too, it is encoded the same way as in SubjectPublicKeyInfo.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature, the public key and the private key are each just a long string of bytes put in a box. The box has no fancy wrapping, and the RFC says exactly which pieces go in and in what order.

sections.title: Key Usage Bits
sections.content:
If a certificate has a keyUsage extension and its public key uses an SLH-DSA identifier, then at least one of digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyCertSign or cRLSign MUST be present.

None of keyEncipherment, dataEncipherment, keyAgreement, encipherOnly or decipherOnly may be present. That makes sense, because SLH-DSA only signs and cannot encrypt or agree on keys. The key usage rules in RFC 5280 still apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A signing stamp can only be used to stamp. The certificate is not allowed to say the key can also lock secret boxes.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Because one OID names both the key and the signature algorithm, a key identified with a Pure SLH-DSA OID is not permitted to make or check a HashSLH-DSA signature, and the reverse is also true. So CA operators must decide in advance which mode a CA certificate will use.

The RFC lists things to weigh. A hardware security module may limit how much data it can take, and SLH-DSA makes two passes over the internal message M', so M' must be held in memory. Large CRLs and end-entity certificates with many subject alternative names may exceed those limits. Verifiers also cannot stream a certificate or CRL, because the randomizer R comes from the signature and must be fed to the digest first. HashSLH-DSA reduces the size of M' that has to be held.

A private key can safely generate a very large number of signatures (2^64). An operator who might approach that should count signatures and destroy the key at a chosen limit, or set the certificate's Not After date so the limit cannot be passed.
sections.plainLanguage: Picking pure or summary signing is like picking a pen before you start, because you cannot switch later. The summary way is easier for small gadgets that cannot hold a huge letter at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SLH-DSA relies on its internal hash and XOF functions being preimage resistant, but not on them being collision resistant. HashSLH-DSA also pre-hashes the message, so it depends on both properties of the pre-hash function. To get enough collision resistance, the pre-hash output is twice the length of the internal hash output.

Implementations MUST protect private keys, because compromise may allow forged signatures. Each key pair MUST be generated independently of all others in the hypertree, and a tree MUST NOT be used for more than 2^64 signing operations. Weak random number generators can leave keys easy to guess.

Fault attacks can lead to forgeries. Verifying a signature before releasing it, the usual countermeasure, is not effective for SLH-DSA, but replicating the signing process is, although signing is already slow. Passive power and emissions side channels can also leak the private key.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep your private stamp locked up, never stamp too many times with one, and make your secret numbers truly random. A sneaky attacker might also try to cause mistakes or listen to the machine hum.
